extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, legal researchers and policymakers interested in Russian law, COVID-19 policy, and misinformation legislation
extracted.subtask_short: overview of Russian COVID-19 fake-news law
extracted.subtask_description: A concise encyclopedic summary of the Russian federal laws (No.99-FZ and No.100-FZ) adopted in spring 2020 that impose administrative and criminal liability for dissemination of 'unreliable information' about threats to life and health (including COVID-19). The page describes statutory amendments, penalties, examples of enforcement, and reactions from rights groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibited conduct — dissemination of 'unreliable information' about threats to life and health
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws establish punishment for the dissemination of "unreliable information" about circumstances that threat to life and health of a citizen including epidemic, natural and technological disasters, emergency, and measures to ensure the security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core substantive prohibition repeated across the statutes; the quoted phrase 'unreliable information' is the statutory trigger for liability and covers statements about epidemics (including COVID-19), disasters, emergencies, and security measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative liability (Federal Law No.99-FZ; Code of Administrative Offenses, article 13.15 parts 10.1 & 10.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal Law No.99-FZ supplemented article 13.15 of the Code of Administrative Offenses with parts 10.1 and 10.2 providing huge administrative fines for natural persons and juridical persons for the dissemination of 'unreliable information' about circumstances that threaten life and health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creates administrative (civil/penal-administrative) sanctions; applies both to individuals (natural persons) and legal entities (juridical persons); characterized in the article as 'huge' fines (no numeric amounts given on the page).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal liability (Federal Law No.100-FZ; Criminal Code articles 207.1 & 207.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal Law No.100-FZ supplemented the Criminal Code with articles 207.1 and 207.2 providing huge criminal fines, forced labour and imprisonment of up to 5 years for natural persons for the dissemination of 'unreliable information' about circumstances that threaten life and health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminal penalties include fines, forced labour and imprisonment (up to 5 years). Criminal provisions attach when the dissemination reaches the statutory threshold of causing or being capable of causing enumerated harms (see separate metric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold for criminal punishment — harms produced or foreseeable
rubrics_metrics.description: Criminal liability applies if such dissemination has produced or could produce human casualties, damage to health of people or to environment, significant material losses, violation of living conditions of the population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These enumerated consequences are the statutory aggravating/triggering conditions for criminal (as opposed to merely administrative) punishment; the law therefore distinguishes between dissemination per se (administrative) and dissemination causing or risking substantial harms (criminal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of subject matter covered by the laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws apply to information concerning epidemics, natural and technological disasters, emergency, and measures to ensure the security — i.e., circumstances that threaten life and health of citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page repeatedly frames the statutes as targeting information about public-health emergencies (explicitly COVID-19) and other wide-scale threats to life/health/security; scope determines whether a given statement falls under the prohibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative aim / stated purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws were aimed at making illegal any doubts as to the nature of COVID-19 and the reasonableness of the measures to combat the epidemic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This description in the article characterizes legislative intent/policy effect — i.e., the laws functioned to suppress doubt or criticism about the disease and government countermeasures. Useful for contextual/legal interpretation and human-rights analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application / enforcement examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported early prosecutions under the new provisions: the first criminal case was opened against activist Anna Shushpanova for a social-media statement; the first conviction was Ekaterina Khrapchenkova for a social-media claim about masks sold in Moscow stores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These concrete enforcement examples illustrate how authorities applied the statutes to social-media posts and the kinds of factual statements that led to charges and conviction; they serve as practical precedent for how the law functions in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reactions and human-rights concerns (criticisms of enforcement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Amnesty International stated authorities prosecuted social media users, journalists and medical professionals for exposing flaws in COVID-19 responses; Freedom House reported additional restrictions on media under the pretext of the pandemic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This documents international NGO criticisms used to evaluate the law's human-rights impact and proportionality; relevant for assessments of freedom of expression, press freedom, and public-interest reporting under the statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to existing 'fake news' legal framework
rubrics_metrics.description: These 2020 statutes are described as an extension of existing Russian fake news laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates the laws should be read in the context of an existing body of 'fake news' legislation in Russia; comparative or cumulative analysis with prior statutes may be necessary when evaluating a particular case.
